A1-A2.headline: The Story Of A Famous Old English Paper

pages.text: In 1215, King John of England faced angry rich lords. They wanted clear limits on the king's power. At Runnymede, both sides agreed to a written deal called Magna Carta to stop war.
pages.caption: The original Magna Carta

imageProvenance.credit: Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound.
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound. (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Magna Carta (British Library Cotton MS Augustus II.106).jpg

pages.text: Later artists painted King John signing the paper with a pen. In truth, he used a heavy wax royal seal in 1215. The peace deal failed fast, and fighting broke out again soon.
pages.caption: A later depiction of the charter

imageProvenance.credit: James William Edmund Doyle / Edmund Evans
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: James William Edmund Doyle / Edmund Evans (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:A Chronicle of England - Page 226 - John Signs the Great Charter.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A romanticised 19th-century recreation of King John signing Magna Carta. Rather than signing in writing, the document would have been authenticated with the Great Seal and applied by officials rather than John himself.

pages.text: In 1216, leaders for young King Henry III shared a new copy without its hardest rules. Later copies kept the deal alive in English life. An old print still shows how the 1215 text looked.
pages.caption: Engraving of the 1215 charter

evidence.articleCaption: 1733 engraving by John Pine of the 1215 charter (Cotton Charter XIII.31A)

pages.text:
Over hundreds of years, the paper's role changed many times. Kings often promised to follow it when they needed money and tax help from lords. People then did not have equal rights.

In the late 1500s and 1600s, lawyers used Magna Carta to stand up to strong kings. Later experts questioned those claims, yet the idea stayed powerful.

These ideas crossed the sea to early American towns and shaped new laws there. Most of the first 1215 rules are no longer used in England today.

Magna Carta did not build modern free rule on its own. Even so, people kept one lasting lesson: even a king must obey the law.

B1-B2.headline: How A Medieval Charter Shaped Modern Democracy And Liberty

pages.text: In 1215, King John faced a revolt from strong English barons who wanted limits on royal power. At Runnymede, Magna Carta offered a written peace deal instead of war, not a modern constitution.
pages.caption: The original Magna Carta

imageProvenance.credit: Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound.

pages.text: Later paintings often show King John signing the charter with a pen. In 1215, officials actually stamped it with the royal seal. The fragile deal soon failed and sparked fresh fighting.
pages.caption: A later depiction of the charter

imageProvenance.credit: James William Edmund Doyle / Edmund Evans
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: James William Edmund Doyle / Edmund Evans (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:A Chronicle of England - Page 226 - John Signs the Great Charter.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A romanticised 19th-century recreation of King John signing Magna Carta. Rather than signing in writing, the document would have been authenticated with the Great Seal and applied by officials rather than John himself.

pages.text: In 1216, leaders for young King Henry III issued a revised copy without its strictest rules. Later versions kept it central in English public life. An engraving still preserves how the 1215 text looked.
pages.caption: Engraving of the 1215 charter

evidence.articleCaption: 1733 engraving by John Pine of the 1215 charter (Cotton Charter XIII.31A)

pages.text:
Over the centuries, Magna Carta's daily role shifted many times. Kings confirmed it to gain tax support in an unequal society where most people had few rights.

By the late 1500s and 1600s, lawyers used the charter as proof of old English rights against strong kings. Later scholars questioned that claim, yet its political pull lasted.

These ideas reached the American colonies and shaped early legal thinking there. Today, almost all of the original 1215 clauses have been removed from English law.

Magna Carta did not build modern democracy on its own. Still, generations kept its core lesson: even rulers must answer to the law.

C1-C2.headline: The Enduring Legacy Of Magna Carta In Global Constitutional History

pages.text: Confronted in 1215 by rebellious English barons demanding constraints on arbitrary crown authority, King John conceded Magna Carta at Runnymede—a pragmatic written settlement aimed at averting civil war rather than a modern constitution.
pages.caption: The original Magna Carta

imageProvenance.credit: Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound.
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Original authors were the barons and King John of England. Uploaded by Earthsound. (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:Magna Carta (British Library Cotton MS Augustus II.106).jpg

pages.text: Although nineteenth-century iconography imagined King John affixing a handwritten signature, medieval chancery practice authenticated the charter with the Great Seal. Rapid papal annulment shattered the truce, reigniting warfare.
pages.caption: A later depiction of the charter

imageProvenance.credit: James William Edmund Doyle / Edmund Evans
imageProvenance.imageAttribution: James William Edmund Doyle / Edmund Evans (Public domain)

evidence.fileTitle: File:A Chronicle of England - Page 226 - John Signs the Great Charter.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: A romanticised 19th-century recreation of King John signing Magna Carta. Rather than signing in writing, the document would have been authenticated with the Great Seal and applied by officials rather than John himself.

pages.text: Henry III's regency strategically reissued a moderated charter in 1216, excising its most radical clauses. Successive confirmations embedded Magna Carta within English governance, while engravings preserved the 1215 text.
pages.caption: Engraving of the 1215 charter

evidence.articleCaption: 1733 engraving by John Pine of the 1215 charter (Cotton Charter XIII.31A)

pages.text:
Throughout medieval governance, monarchs periodically reconfirmed Magna Carta in exchange for parliamentary tax subsidies within a stratified society of unequal privileges.

By the late sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, jurists invoked it as ancient constitutional liberty opposing absolutism; despite later revisionism, its influence endured.

Transatlantic legal discourse transplanted Magna Carta's ideals into North American colonial charters and constitutional thought, even as British statutes repealed nearly all original clauses.

While the compact neither instituted modern democracy nor universal rights, generations elevated its enduring maxim: sovereign power must answer to law.
